5. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff petitioner submits that the judgment of the learned appellate court below is not a proper judgment of reversal because the appellate court below being the final court of fact has not controverts the reasoning and discussion of the trial court inasmuch as the learned appellate court below has not considered and discussed the entire evidence oral and documentary on record and as such this error of law on the part of the appellate court below caused erroneous decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that 'the learned appellate court below misread the C.S. khatian No. 261 exhibit 3 C in asmuch as he failed to read the word “গং” after Sonaton Baroi and also failed to read the word “বরাত” in C.S. Khatian No. 76 and the total non-consideration of these material words vitiated the findings of the appellate court below. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned appellate court below erred in law in deciding the question of title of the suit plot in favour of the defendants by wrongly holding that the properties of the disputed C.S. Khatian 76 exhibit 3C belong to Sonaton Baroi, the predecessor of the defendants along although it has been held that the suit is not maintainable for its involvement of complicated question of title. The learned Advocate referring to exhibit 3B and 3C further submits that the learned appellate Court below erred in holding that the learned Munsif is not justified to observe that the land originally belonged to Sonaton Baroi and Ramananda Baroi in equal shares. The learned Advocate with much emphasis submits that the learned appellate court below failed to consider and discuss the various exhibited documents filed by the plaintiff petitioner such as exhibits 1,1A, 2-2A, 3, 3A, 3B, 4A, 5, 6, 6A and also the oral evidence of 5 P.Ws. and those have proved the plaintiff's title and possession in the suit land and as such there is erroneous decision in the matter by the appellate court below occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that exhibit IA, bainapatra and exhibit 3A, S.A. Khatian, exhibit 2-2A rent receipts, exhibit 3 R.S. khatian exhibit 4, 4A containing an admission of Satya Ranjan son of Randha Ballav about the possession and title of the plaintiff petitioner's vendors in the suit plot and evidence of P.Ws. clearly proved the plaintiff's possession and title in the suit land and as such the learned appellate court contrary to those evidence on record erred in dismissing the suit. The learned Advocate finally submits that the defendants could not produce their alleged bainapatra dated 6.11.1963 showing their alleged possession since 1963 and that the defendants case of possession being self contradictory and that D.W.1 and 2 could not give the boundary of the suit plot inasmuch as D.W.1 and 2 are the defendant Nos. 1 and 4 respectively and as such the appellate court below erred in setting aside the decision of the trial court which decreed the suit considering the evidence and materials of the plaintiff vis-a-vis those of the defendants. Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, the learned Advocate, in support of his contention refers to and relies on the decisions namely (1991)11 BLD (AD)245,37D.L.R.79,PLD1976 (SC)784, 35DLR216 and 6 DLR 271. 

 22. One of the grievances of Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur is that the impugned judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal. The learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner has argued that the impugned judgment passed by the appellate court below is not a proper judgment of reversal in as much as the object of the Rule 31 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure has not been complied with by the appellate court below. This contention of the learned Advocate for the plaintiff petitioner appears to be well founded. The object of Rule 31 of Order 41 of the Code is to see that a Judge does not act callously or even mechanically. Its purpose is to put the Judge on the right track and to the extent Rule of Procedure can do it, to see that he acts judicially. It enables the High Court to Judge whether the appellate court below had independently considered the case with a consciousness of relevant points which arose for adjudication. It is also to afford the parties opportunity of knowing the grounds of decision to enable them to exercise the right of revision and to enable the High Court Division in revision to see whether lower appellate court has properly appreciated and decided the case. Appellate judgment reversing the judgment of trial court should be adequate and satisfactory. It must contain definite findings on the questions involved and must give reasons for reversing the decisions of the trial court. In fact judgment of reversal may often need a little more discussion of facts, evidence and points involved in the case so as to embody in it convincing reasons for reversing the findings of the courts of first instance. It should cover almost entire grounds covered by the judgment appealed from. It must express opinion on all points on which the lower court has based its conclusion. It is not necessary for lower appellate court to mention each and every particular item of evidence in its judgment provided it is clear upon reading of the judgment itself that all relevant evidence has been substantially considered by the appellate court below. The appellate judgment may not meet all reasons given in the judgment of the trial court while setting it aside. The appellate court must advert to the findings and reasoning’s assigned by the trial court. These principles had not been followed by the appellate court below in as much as in some places appellate court grossly misread the evidence and the impugned judgment suffers from non-reading and non-consideration of the materials and evidence on record. The trial court discussed the evidence on the point of possession with regard to both oral and documentary evidence and after close scrutiny of the same have relied on the testimonies of the P.Ws. and discarded the testimonies of the D.Ws. on that point. The appellate court below failed to consider the assertions made by the parties in respect of possession of the suit property and also failed to notice the fact that in the instant case the defendants have failed to produce the agreement by virtue of which they have filed Title Suit No. 77 of 1969 and got an exparte decree and they have not been able to prove the said agreement even in the instant case. The learned appellate court below also failed to take notice of the fact that the case of possession is self contradictory inasmuch as in the said suit for specific performance of contract the defendant opposite parties have asserted that they have entered into possession of the suit land in 1963 in pursuance of bainapatra whereas in his evidence the D.W. 1 who is the defendant No. 1 asserted that they entered into possession of the suit land, through the court after execution of the decree of Title Suit No. 77 of 1974. The trial court dealt with the matter in detail but the learned appellate court below did not advert to it in its judgment. In 14 BLD (AD)229 it has been held by their Lordship that the appellate court whether reversing or affirming the decision of the trial court must independently consider the evidence on record but in the case of affirming the findings of the trial court, the narration of the entire evidence and reiteration of the reasons given by the trial court are not essential. In such a case expressions of general agreement with those of the trial court are generally considered sufficient. But in the case of reversal of the judgment the consideration of the evidence, of necessity, has to be thoroughly and more elaborate. But in the instant case it is crystal clear from the impugned judgment that the learned appellate court below failed to advert to the evidences both oral and documentary adduced by the plaintiff petitioner and the learned appellate court below also failed to reverse the finding of the trial court by giving cogent reason therefor. It has been held in the case reported in 15 BLD (AD) 120 that while exercising revisional power under section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code the High Court usually does not go into the question of fact but when the appellate court reverse the judgment of the trial court on non consideration of the materials on record and without adverting to the reasoning on which the trial court gave its judgment, the High Court may be justified to interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the appellate court when it finds that non-consideration of such evidence has materially affected the appellate court judgment occasioning failure of justice. In the light of the aforesaid principles of law also the impugned judgment cannot be sustained in law.
